prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Right, When, They

outputs.L1:
**Untitled**
*January, 1990*

I tell my attendants, *Right there,*
When they rub me where it itches.
They rub for a few seconds, then move on—
There is so much of it to wash,
"It" being me, a former person,
Now something that must be washed each day
In so little time.

Fifty minutes beyond my breathing machine,
And all I can do is stare
As my breath recedes like the woman
Who would not love me.

*It's almost over,* I say over and over to myself
The moment the machine falls silent.
An idiotic mantra, perhaps,
But it helps when the ache descends into my eyes
And my words no longer come out right.

*Left hand,* I say.
*Right foot?* the attendant ventures, guessing.

I begin to dream of gusts of air
Rushing down my windpipe with hurricane force—
Garish and impossible, they are respiratory porn.
My re-entry is stalled
By the attendant smoothing a sheet
That no one will ever see.
Enraged, I clench my eyes shut.
*Christ.*
"What?"
*Never mind.*

Once back inside and switched on,
I cough violently, and with conviction.
Startled by the force of the inrushing air,
I feel my lungs expand like birthday balloons,
My terror-flattened mind springs up into 3-D,
As I return to the land of breathing.

---

I've refined the phrasing for flow and eloquence—smoothing transitions, sharpening word choices ("beyond" for "outside," "the moment...falls silent" for "as soon as...turned off," "ventures" for "says," "clench...shut" for "squeeze...closed," "springs" for "pops")—while preserving every image, line, and piece of information from your original. Let me know if you'd prefer a lighter touch or a different tone.
outputs.L2:
I give directions to my caregivers, telling them "There, that spot," whenever they scratch the place that itches. After a couple seconds of scratching, they continue on—there's such a large surface to clean. That "surface" is my own body, once a whole human being, now merely an object requiring daily cleansing within a cramped window of time.

I get fifty minutes away from my ventilator, and during that stretch I'm helpless, only able to gaze upward while my breath drains away from me—much like the woman who refused to return my love.

The moment they shut off the machine, I keep repeating to myself, *It's nearly finished.* Maybe it's a foolish little chant, but it gives me comfort when the pain sinks into my eyes and I can no longer speak clearly.

"Left hand," I try to say.

"Right foot?" my caregiver responds, taking a guess.

I start imagining powerful blasts of air storming down my throat with the strength of a hurricane. These visions are extravagant and unattainable—pure fantasy for someone starved of breath.

My return gets delayed while the caregiver smooths out a bedsheet that no one will even look at. Furious, I clench my eyelids shut.

*God.*

"What?"

*Forget it.*

Finally reconnected and switched back on, I cough hard and deliberately. The rush of air catches me off guard with its power, and I feel my lungs swelling like party balloons. My mind, pressed flat by fear, springs back into full dimension as I come home to the world of breathing.

January, 1990
outputs.L3:
# Life at the Edge of Breath

There is a particular kind of dehumanization that comes with being cared for. Each day, my caretaking routine reminds me that I have become, in some essential way, less than I once was. I have started to think of myself as a former person—no longer a full human being, but rather an object to be tended to, a thing that must be washed and maintained. The intimacy of being handled, cleaned, and moved strips away something I cannot name but deeply miss. What remains feels like the residue of the man I used to be.

My survival depends entirely on a breathing machine. Without it, I have fifty minutes—no more. During those minutes, I watch my breath recede from me like a tide pulling away from shore, and I am helpless to stop it. There is nothing to do but observe my own diminishment, feeling the anxiety build as each breath grows shallower and more precious than the last.

To survive the terror of those minutes, I have learned to repeat a single phrase: *It's almost over.* I say it to myself again and again, a desperate mantra that becomes my only handhold as the physical distress intensifies. The words do not make the suffering disappear, but they give me something to cling to—a promise that the ordeal has an end, that relief is coming, that I only have to endure a little longer.

Communication with my attendants offers little comfort. My words fail me when I need them most. I try to make simple requests, and they are misunderstood; I ask for one thing and receive another. The frustration of not being able to make myself known—of being trapped behind language that no longer obeys me—adds another layer to the isolation of my condition.

And then, at last, I am reconnected to the machine. The return of breath is violent, almost brutal in its suddenness—but it is relief above all else. I feel my body seize the air, my mind flickering back to life as oxygen floods through me once more. In that moment, I cross back over the threshold and re-enter what I have come to think of as the land of breathing. I am alive again. For now, that is enough.
outputs.L4:
They come for me each morning at the same hour, and each morning I brace myself the only way I can—inside my own skull, where I am still able to move.

The washing begins. Two of them roll me, and the sheet slides beneath my back like something being pulled from under a fallen tree. A warm cloth, then a cool one, then the ammonia-bright smell of whatever they use on the parts of me I can no longer feel as mine. I have learned not to watch their faces while they work. There is a particular expression people wear when they clean a body that cannot thank them, a careful blankness, and it is worse to witness than any cruelty. So I look at the ceiling tile with the water stain shaped like Portugal, and I begin the mantra.

*I am still here. I am still here. I am still here.*

It is not a prayer, exactly. It is a rope I throw across the widening gap between the man I was and the object I have become. Because they must disconnect me now. This is the part.

Fifty minutes. Every day, fifty minutes off the ventilator, so the machine can be checked, so the tubing can be changed, so someone in an office somewhere can be satisfied that the protocol has been followed. Fifty minutes in which the great artificial lung that breathes for me falls silent, and I am handed back my own drowning.

The panic comes first, always. A hot animal thing that starts in the chest and climbs. My diaphragm makes its small, useless efforts, a bird beating against glass. This is when the fantasies begin, because the mantra alone cannot hold. I imagine air. Not gentle air—rushing air, a torrent of it, cold and clean and roaring down a mountainside straight into me. I picture standing on a cliff with my mouth open to a gale. I picture opening the door of a plane. I fill myself, in my mind, with more air than any lung could hold, birthday balloons and storm winds and the whole blue weight of the sky.

The mind does strange things when it is starved. Time flattens. Colors dim at the edges. The room seems to recede, to become a photograph of a room, and I of it. I feel myself thinning, becoming two-dimensional, a drawing of a man on a bed, a diagram in a textbook labeled *former person*. This is the true terror of it—not the suffocation, but the sense that I am being erased, wiped down and put away like the cleaned instruments, reduced to a thing that must simply be maintained. A body on a list. An item to be preserved until it is no longer worth preserving.

And then—the click.

The connection is remade. The machine draws its first breath through me, and my lungs expand like birthday balloons, all at once, gloriously, absurdly, and the world snaps back into three dimensions. The water stain on the ceiling has depth again. The light has weight. I can hear the small sounds of the corridor, a cart, a laugh, a life going on. I am flooded, revived, dragged back up through the flat gray water into color and volume and the improbable fact of my continuing.

I am still here.

The relief is so total that it frightens me almost as much as the drowning did, because it shows me exactly how thin the rope is, how narrow the margin between the man thinking these words and the silence that waits fifty minutes at a time to take him. I survive by machine and by mantra and by imagining wind. Tomorrow they will come at the same hour, and I will look at Portugal on the ceiling, and I will begin again.

# Standing Up at the Right Moment

There comes a time in everyone's life when the decision to act feels almost impossible. We hesitate, we wait, and we wonder if the moment will ever truly be **right**. Yet, experience teaches us that perfect conditions rarely arrive on their own.

## Knowing When to Act

The hardest part of any challenge is recognizing **when** to move forward. Too often, people delay important choices, believing that tomorrow will bring more clarity or courage. But timing is a delicate art. Sometimes the **right** decision is not about waiting for the ideal circumstances—it is about seizing the opportunity that stands before you.

Consider how successful individuals approach obstacles. **When** they face uncertainty, they trust their preparation and instincts. They understand that hesitation can cost them more than a bold, imperfect action.

## The Power of "They"

We often look to others—those we admire—and think about how **they** managed to overcome their struggles. **They** were not gifted with special luck; instead, **they** learned to embrace risk. When we study the paths of people who inspire us, we realize **they** simply chose to begin, even when success was not guaranteed.

## Finding Your Own Right Time

In the end, the **right** moment is the one you create. **When** you commit fully to your goals, and when you stop waiting for permission, you join the ranks of those who make things happen. **They** are not different from you—**they** simply decided that the time was now.

So ask yourself: is this the **right** moment? And **when** you find the answer, act with confidence, just as **they** did before you.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free verse poem from the perspective of a person with severe paralysis or a respiratory condition who spends limited time off a breathing machine, capturing the physical vulnerability and frustration of being washed and tended by attendants.
counterfactuals.output:
# Between Breaths

They come with warm cloths and careful hands,
and I am an island they navigate—
turning me, cresting my hip like a wave
they've mapped a hundred times.

The machine sighs behind me,
patient, waiting to take me back.
I have forty minutes.
Forty minutes of borrowed air
before the tightness climbs my chest
like ivy reclaiming a wall.

*Lift your arm*, she says,
gentle, and I cannot.
I want to tell her—
once these arms rowed boats,
once they lifted children overhead
into the shattering light of ordinary afternoons.

Now they lift me
the way you'd move a sleeping thing,
tender and impersonal,
and I float in the strangeness
of being touched everywhere
and reaching nothing.

The washcloth finds the hollow of my throat.
I am clean. I am cared for.
I am a country occupied by kindness
and I resent the flag they plant
in the territory of my own skin—

not them, never them,
their hands are good,
but the *arrangement* of it,
the arithmetic of dignity
divided by dependence.

Somewhere a clock.
Somewhere my lungs begin their small rebellion,
the panic that is not panic
but the body's honest math:
*not enough, not enough.*

Bring it back, I think,
the mask, the rhythm, the mechanical mercy—
and I hate that I want it,
hate that relief and imprisonment
wear the same plastic face.

They tuck the sheet.
They smooth my hair
the way you'd finish a made bed,
and I am grateful,
I am furious,
I am a man made mostly of waiting

who once, I swear it,
held his breath on purpose
just to feel the sweetness
of letting it go.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a confessional poem set in January 1990 about a disabled narrator's daily routine of being bathed and briefly separated from a ventilator, using dark humor and vivid imagery like "respiratory porn" and lungs expanding like birthday balloons.
counterfactuals.output:
# Ninety Seconds in January

The nurse arrives at seven with her sponge
and revolution—unhooks me from the machine
that breathes so I don't have to, this small plunge
into the naked air, this in-between.

Ninety seconds. That's my whole allowance
of unassisted living, my brief parole.
The ventilator sighs its disavowance
like a lover watching me walk out the door.

*Respiratory porn,* I call it, when
my lungs expand like birthday balloons, obscene
and desperate, blown up by borrowed men
in scrubs who've seen more of me than I have seen.

The water's warm. She scrubs the parts of me
that can't feel scrubbing—territories lost,
a map of numb geography.
January light. The window's edged in frost.

I count the seconds like a diver would,
each one a pearl I'm not allowed to keep.
My chest performs its little brotherhood
of muscle, memory, the ancient sleep

of doing this alone. *You're doing great,*
she lies, and towels the borrowed heat away.
The machine reclaims me. I capitulate
to plastic lungs. We'll do this all tomorrow, same

blue hour, same sponge, same ninety-second joke
where I'm the punchline and the setup both—
a body that forgot the way to choke
on its own air, that broke its solemn oath

to breathe. She tucks me in. The bellows hiss
resumes its steady, mechanical amen.
I've been undressed, rebreathed, reduced to this:
alive, on loan, and grateful. Count again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem exploring the experience of dependency on caregivers, including miscommunication between the speaker and attendants, terror about breathing, and a lost love, ending with the relief of returning to the machine.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Machine and I**

They lift me like a question
they've forgotten how to ask,
their hands professional, kind, wrong—
turning me a quarter-inch
from the ache I couldn't name,
into a new one.

*No,* I say, *not there,*
but the word arrives too late,
already they are smoothing sheets,
already they've decided
what my silence meant.

Between us: a country
with no shared language,
only the pantomime of need,
the guesswork of the body
translated badly, twice.

And underneath it all
the old terror rising—
that stutter in the chest,
the animal counting
each breath like coins
it cannot spare to lose.

I have learned to fear the pause,
the interval where air
might simply not arrive,
where the lungs forget
their single, stubborn verb.

I think of him sometimes.
How once my breathing
was a thing he listened for
across a dark room,
proof enough that I remained.
How love, too, was a kind of air
I did not know I'd stop receiving.

He is elsewhere now,
breathing for himself alone,
and I am here,
being handled into evening,
misheard, adjusted,
almost understood.

But then the hour turns.
They fit the mask, they seal me
back into the rhythm
that does not misinterpret,
that asks for nothing,
grants me the one clean gift—

the machine that breathes me,
patient, tireless, sure,
its low mechanical hymn
saying *in, and out, and in,*
the only fluent tongue
that never gets me wrong.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a first-person narrative poem about someone who feels reduced to "a former person" who must be washed daily, blending bodily helplessness, rage, and the desperate anticipation of drawing breath again.
counterfactuals.output:
# What Remains

They come with basins, warm and blue,
these hands that are not mine to hold—
they lift the arm that used to do
the work of me. Now I am told

*there, there,* as if I were a child,
as if the *there* could reach the place
where I still burn, still churning wild
behind this slackened, nodding face.

The washcloth finds my collarbone.
I feel it. Understand—I feel
each drop, each stranger's touch, each tone
of pity poured. And this is real:

I rage. Inside this ruined coast
of body, something stands and screams—
not gratitude, not quiet ghost,
but *me*, the wreckage of my dreams,

who once could run, could reach, could turn
a doorknob, drink, could simply *be*
without an audience to learn
the map of my indignity.

They dip. They wring. They speak above
my head as though I've gone away.
*A former person.* No—my love,
I'm here. I'm listening. Every day

I hoard the seconds. Watch. I wait
for that one thing they cannot take:
the pause before the chest inflates,
the pull, the pause, the rising ache—

and then it comes. The lungs unfold.
Air floods the dark and holds me whole.
*Still breathing.* Furious. Not old
enough to end. I keep my soul

between the exhale and the next,
a tenant of that narrow door.
They wash a body. Leave me vexed,
alive, and burning. *Still.* Once more.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poignant poem about life on a respirator, weaving in fantasies of powerful rushing air, an "idiotic mantra" to endure the ache, and the violent cough of re-entry into breathing.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Machine That Breathes for Me

Each hiss and sigh, a stranger's rhythm keeps
this borrowed cadence in my hollow chest—
a bellows working while my body sleeps,
insisting still, *inhale*, then *exhale*, *rest*.

I dream of wind that never asks permission:
the wild Atlantic gusts that flatten grass,
the storm-front's roar, the mountain's cold ambition,
great rushing walls of air I'll never pass

through lungs that once were mine. Now I recite
the idiotic mantra, *hold, endure,
just count the tiles, just make it through the night,*
as if such nonsense offered any cure

for aching ribs that rise on someone else's beat.
I bargain with the ceiling, count to ten,
I tell myself the litany's complete—
*one breath, one more, and then, and then, and then—*

Until the weaning comes. They pull the tube.
The world caves in. My throat, a ragged door
flung open to a hurricane, the crude
and violent cough that wracks me to the floor

of my own flesh. I heave. I gag. I claw
raw fistfuls of the ordinary air—
this savage, holy, unremarkable law
of drawing breath, that I once did not care

to notice. Now each swallow is a war
I win by inches, gasping, wet, and torn,
alive against the odds, and wanting more
of what it costs to be, again, newborn.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
